plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a labeled cross-sectional diagram of a Hall-Héroult electrolytic cell used for the industrial production of aluminum metal from Al2O3 dissolved in molten cryolite (Na3AlF6). The outermost structure consists of a steel shell lined with ceramic insulation; inside, two large rectangular carbon anodes (+) are suspended from above into a green-tinted electrolyte layer representing Al2O3 dissolved in molten Na3AlF6, while a sloped carbon cathode (−) forms the entire floor of the cell. White dots surrounding the anodes represent bubbles of O2, CO, and CO2 that form as the carbon anodes are oxidized during electrolysis, and molten aluminum — reduced from Al3+ at the cathode — collects as a dense liquid layer above the cathode floor; a solid crust of electrolyte forms at the top surface of the melt. Gaseous HF and particulates generated during operation are routed upward through an exhaust line labeled "HF and particulates exhaust to filter plant," reflecting the environmental management demands of the process. This figure establishes the Hall-Héroult cell as the primary industrial route for aluminum smelting, highlighting how dissolving Al2O3 in molten Na3AlF6 lowers the operating temperature below what pure Al2O3 would require and how the simultaneous oxidation of the carbon anodes produces mixed gaseous byproducts.

interactionPlan.concept: The Hall-Héroult cell produces aluminum by reducing dissolved Al3+ at the carbon cathode while oxidizing oxide ions at consumable carbon anodes, generating molten aluminum and exhaust gases.

interactions.teaches: Students see that aluminum forms at the cathode while oxide-derived gases form at the anodes, so the two half-reactions occur in different places.
interactions.label: Animate electrolysis

interactions.teaches: Students understand that higher current drives faster electrolysis, producing more gas bubbles and a faster-growing molten aluminum layer.
interactions.label: Applied current

interactions.teaches: Students connect the cell’s inputs and outputs: alumina enters the molten electrolyte, aluminum collects at the bottom, and gaseous byproducts are exhausted to filtration.
interactions.label: Trace material flow

demo_steps.title: Identify the cell layers
demo_steps.narration: The steel shell and ceramic lining contain a hot molten electrolyte of Al2O3 dissolved in cryolite. The carbon anodes hang into the electrolyte, while the carbon cathode forms the floor.

demo_steps.title: Start electrolysis
demo_steps.narration: When current flows, Al3+ ions are reduced at the negative carbon cathode and become molten aluminum. The dense liquid aluminum collects as a layer above the cathode floor.

demo_steps.title: Watch the anodes react
demo_steps.narration: Oxide ions are oxidized at the positive carbon anodes. Because the anodes are carbon, the oxygen forms bubbles of O2, CO, and CO2 rather than simply collecting as pure oxygen.

demo_steps.title: Increase the current
demo_steps.narration: Raising the applied current increases the rate of electrolysis. More bubbles appear near the anodes, and the molten aluminum pool thickens more quickly.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Aluminum is produced at the cathode, but the carbon anodes are consumed as oxide ions are converted into gaseous byproducts.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate a clean cross-sectional industrial cell diagram with a dark gray outer steel container, peach ceramic lining, green electrolyte bath, black carbon electrodes, and a gray molten aluminum layer at the bottom. Keep the two large carbon anodes centered and suspended from a top positive busbar, with white bubble clusters concentrated around their sides and lower edges. Show the cathode as a sloped black floor labeled with a negative sign, and include the exhaust duct and upward arrow above the cell. Labels should sit outside the cell with leader lines, matching the original emphasis on crust, electrolyte, molten aluminum, bubbles, ceramic, steel shell, anodes, cathode, and exhaust. The animation overlay should use small colored ion markers and arrows without obscuring the original labels; the material-flow toggle should add clear feed, product, and exhaust arrows.

authoredContext:
The preparation of aluminum utilizes a process invented in 1886 by Charles M. Hall , who began to work on the problem while a student at Oberlin College in Ohio. Paul L. T. Héroult discovered the process independently a month or two later in France. In honor to the two inventors, this electrolysis cell is known as the Hall–Héroult cell . The Hall–Héroult cell is an electrolysis cell for the production of aluminum. illustrates the Hall–Héroult cell.

The next step is to remove the precipitated aluminum hydroxide by filtration. Heating the hydroxide produces aluminum oxide, Al 2 O 3 , which dissolves in a molten mixture of cryolite, Na 3 AlF 6 , and calcium fluoride, CaF 2 . Electrolysis of this solution takes place in a cell like that shown in . Reduction of aluminum ions to the metal occurs at the cathode, while oxygen, carbon monoxide, and carbon dioxide form at the anode.

An electrolytic cell is used for the production of aluminum. The electrolysis of a solution of cryolite and calcium fluoride results in aluminum metal at the cathode, and oxygen, carbon monoxide, and carbon dioxide at the anode.

A diagram is shown. At the center of the diagram are two black squares, each labeled, “Carbon anode ( positive sign ),” and connected by forked tubes to a horizontal tube labeled with a positive sign. The carbon anodes are submerged in a green liquid labeled, “A l subscript 2 O subscript 3 dissolved in molten N a subscript 3 A l F subscript 6.” It is held in place by a three-sided, double layered container which is labeled, “Steel sheet,” on the outer layer and, “Ceramic,” on the inner layer. The carbon anodes are surrounded by bubbles labeled, “Bubbles of O subscript 2, C O, and C O subscript 2.” Below the green liquids lies a silver layer labeled, “Molten aluminum,” and a black layer labeled, “Carbon cathode ( negative sign ).” Above the diagram is an outlet tube labeled with an upward-facing arrow and the words, “H F and particulates exhaust to filter plant.”
